title: CAN A SINGLE CHRISTIAN HAVE MANY BOYFRIENDS OR GIRLFRIENDS?
paragraphs:
CAN A SINGLE CHRISTIAN HAVE MANY BOYFRIENDS OR GIRLFRIENDS?
You may call it “keeping your options open.” But what happens when several hearts are being held by promises you were never prepared to keep?
There is a kind of heartbreak nobody talks about in church.
It happens before marriage.
Sometimes before an official relationship even exists.
Two people talk every night.
They pray together.
They share things they have never told anyone else.
“Good morning” becomes expected.
“Good night” becomes intimate.
There are pet names. Jealousy. Flirting. Emotional dependence. Private promises. Future plans disguised as jokes.
One person says, “We’re not technically together.”
But the other person’s heart has already started living as though they are.
Then comes the revelation.
There is someone else.
Maybe two.
Maybe three.
And suddenly the sentence appears:
“But I’m single. I’m allowed to talk to whoever I want.”
Legally? Perhaps.
Technically? Perhaps.
But the Christian life has never been merely about asking:
“How much can I technically get away with before it becomes sin?”
Jesus calls us to something much deeper.
The question is not merely, “Am I officially single?”
The question is:
“Am I loving these people in a way that looks like Jesus?”
And that changes everything.
Because Scripture does not contain a verse saying, “Thou shalt not have three people you are casually dating.”
The modern boyfriend-girlfriend system did not exist in exactly the form we know today.
So we have to be careful.
We must not manufacture commandments God did not give.
But neither should we pretend Scripture has nothing to say simply because the Bible does not use our modern dating vocabulary.
Scripture gives us something far more penetrating than a dating rulebook.
It gives us the character of Christ.
And once His character enters the conversation, our excuses begin losing oxygen.
Paul writes:
The Greek is painfully direct:
ἡ ἀγάπη τῷ πλησίον κακὸν οὐκ ἐργάζεται
Hē agapē tō plēsion kakon ouk ergazetai.
In context, the idea is that love does not work evil or harm toward one’s neighbor.
Notice what Paul does not say.
Love does no harm only after engagement.
Love does no harm only after becoming Facebook official.
Love does no harm only after exclusivity has been verbally established.
No.
Christian love asks what our behavior is doing to another human being.

That means a single Christian may certainly meet people, develop friendships, discern compatibility, and—in cultures where this is normal—even go on early dates with more than one person before exclusivity has been established.
That fact by itself is not automatically sexual immorality or adultery.
We should not call something sin merely because we personally dislike it.
But there is an enormous difference between honest non-exclusive discernment and collecting romantic attachments.
There is a difference between:
“I’m getting to know people, and everyone understands that I have not entered an exclusive relationship,”
and:
“I am making several people feel chosen because I enjoy being desired by all of them.”
One can involve transparent discernment.
The other can become deception dressed in the language of freedom.
And maybe that is where this article just touched a nerve.
Because perhaps you do not have several boyfriends.
You just have several people who think they might eventually become your boyfriend.
Perhaps you do not call them girlfriends.
You simply give multiple women enough emotional intimacy to keep them hoping.
One gets your late-night vulnerability.
One gets your flirting.
One gets your physical affection.
One gets your spiritual conversations.
One gets your “maybe someday.”
And whenever somebody asks what this actually is, you retreat behind the safest sentence available:
“We’re just friends.”
But are you treating them like friends?
That is the harder question.
Because you can remain technically single while becoming emotionally dishonest.
You can avoid the word “relationship” while enjoying nearly every emotional privilege of one.
You can keep someone close enough to feed your loneliness but far enough away that you never have to become responsible for what you are awakening in their heart.
And Christians are not called merely to avoid technical adultery.
We are called to walk in truth.
Paul says in Ephesians 4:25:
“Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor.”
The Greek phrase includes:
λαλεῖτε ἀλήθειαν
laleite alētheian—
speak truth.
Truthfulness is bigger than avoiding explicit lies.
You can deceive someone without saying the sentence, “I am lying to you.”
Sometimes deception happens through carefully maintained ambiguity.
You know they think they are special.
You know they believe this is heading somewhere.
You know they would be devastated if they saw how you speak to somebody else.
Yet you keep receiving their affection because it feels good to be wanted.
That deserves examination before God.
Not because attraction is evil.
Not because singleness is shameful.
Not because dating is dirty.
But because people are not emotional vending machines created to dispense affirmation whenever loneliness hits.
They bear the image of God.
And if you are serious about following Jesus, you cannot ask only:
“What am I allowed to take from this relationship?”
You eventually have to ask:
“How can I honor this person before Christ?”
Paul gives another astonishingly practical command:
“Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor.” — Romans 12:10
The Greek word translated “honor” is:
τιμή — timē
It carries the sense of honor, value, esteem.
Imagine what Christian dating would become if that became the question.
Not:
“How many options can I maintain?”
Not:
“How many people find me attractive?”
Not:
“How long can I keep this undefined?”
But:
“Am I treating this person as someone of value before God?”
That question reaches the man secretly maintaining five flirtatious conversations.
It reaches the woman keeping three men emotionally attached because she fears choosing the wrong one.
It reaches the person who says, “I never promised anything,” while knowing perfectly well that their behavior communicated something their mouth carefully avoided saying.
It also reaches the wounded Christian doing this because somebody once did it to them.
Maybe you were abandoned.
Maybe you were cheated on.
Maybe someone promised forever and disappeared.
Maybe now you keep several people around because having options feels safer than vulnerability.
If one leaves, there is another.
If one rejects you, somebody else still wants you.
If one stops texting, another notification protects you from silence.
It feels like power.
But sometimes what looks like romantic freedom is actually fear wearing expensive perfume.
You are not choosing several people because you love deeply.
You are keeping several doors open because you are terrified of standing in one doorway long enough to be rejected.
Jesus sees that wound too.
And His answer is not humiliation.
His answer is truth and grace.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity is not the story of morally impressive people learning better dating etiquette.
It is the story of sinners being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have played with hearts.
Maybe you have lied.
Maybe you have used somebody physically.
Maybe you have kept someone emotionally attached while secretly pursuing someone else.
Maybe you crossed sexual boundaries and then used “we aren’t married” as permission.
Scripture does speak clearly about sexual holiness.
Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “sexual immorality” is:
πορνεία — porneia
In New Testament usage, it refers broadly to sexual immorality.
Then Paul continues with something our culture desperately needs to hear:
“that no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter.” — 1 Thessalonians 4:6
Sexual holiness is therefore not merely about rules concerning your own body.
It also concerns how your desires affect another person.
God cares about bodies.
God cares about hearts.
God cares about truth.
God cares about the person you are touching.
God cares about the person you are promising yourself to.
God cares about the person whose affection you are receiving.
And God cares about you.
That is why biblical boundaries are not evidence that God hates romance.
They are evidence that God understands its power.
Sexual and romantic intimacy can bind memories to people.
It can awaken expectations.
It can produce profound vulnerability.
It can leave wounds that continue speaking years after a relationship ends.
So should single Christians date several people?
Here is the careful biblical answer:

Scripture does not explicitly prohibit a single Christian from initially getting to know more than one potential spouse when there has been no commitment to exclusivity and everyone involved understands the situation honestly.
But Scripture absolutely confronts deception, selfishness, sexual immorality, exploitation, dishonesty, manipulation, and failure to love our neighbor.

Therefore, if “having many boyfriends or girlfriends” means maintaining multiple simultaneous committed romantic relationships while each person reasonably believes they have your exclusive devotion, deception has entered the picture.
If it means keeping several people romantically attached without honest disclosure because you enjoy the attention, you need to examine your heart.
If it means sexual involvement outside marriage, Scripture calls you toward sexual holiness.

And if it simply means transparently meeting different people while prayerfully discerning marriage before making an exclusive commitment, Christians should be careful not to create a commandment where Scripture itself does not give one.
But there is still another question.
A more uncomfortable one.
Why do you need so many people wanting you?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit there for a moment.
Why does losing romantic attention frighten you so much?
Why does an unanswered message make you feel invisible?
Why does being desired make you feel valuable?
Why does being alone make you wonder whether something is wrong with you?
Maybe the deepest issue was never how many people you are allowed to date.
Maybe the deepest issue is that you have been asking human affection to tell you something only God can finally settle.
“Am I worth loving?”
And into that ache comes Jesus Christ.
Not another match.
Not another notification.
Not another admirer.
Jesus.
The One who knew the worst chapter before He called your name.
The One who does not discover your hidden history after falling in love with a polished version of you.
He already knows.
And still the Gospel says:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
While we were still sinners.
Not after the profile was cleaned.
Not after the secret conversations were deleted.
Not after the lust disappeared.
Not after you finally became marriage material.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not excuse sin.
It destroys our excuse for remaining in it.
Grace is not Jesus whispering, “Keep using people. It doesn’t matter.”
Grace is Jesus saying:
“Come out of hiding. I paid too much for you to keep calling your chains freedom.”
Repentance is not self-hatred.
The New Testament word is:
μετάνοια — metanoia
It speaks of repentance, a turning of mind and heart toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
Real grace can produce real change.
So perhaps today your repentance looks painfully practical.
You stop maintaining romantic backups.
You tell somebody the truth.
You apologize without demanding forgiveness.
You end the sexual relationship you know dishonors Christ.
You stop flirting with someone you have no intention of pursuing.
You stop calling manipulation “being friendly.”
You stop demanding relationship privileges from someone you refuse to commit to.
You stop treating people like insurance policies against loneliness.
And perhaps, for the first time in years, you become single in the deepest sense.
Not abandoned.
Not unwanted.
Not forgotten.
Simply no longer using another human being to prove that you matter.
Then you discover something terrifyingly beautiful:
Jesus is still there.
Maybe you recognize yourself in these words.
Do not hide.
There is no trophy for pretending.
The Church should be a place where sinners can step into the light and discover that Jesus still saves sinners.
And maybe someone on your Facebook friends list desperately needs this truth.
Because loneliness has a strange ability to make yesterday’s convictions negotiable tomorrow night.
And there is more than content behind this mission.
If you are tired of shallow Christianity...
If you want Scripture that confronts you and grace that brings you home...
If you want biblical nourishment, accountability, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual sharpening centered on Jesus Christ...
Stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the lukewarm.
Invite the seeker.
Even invite the person who says they do not believe.
But before you leave, remember the question with which we began.
Can a single Christian have many boyfriends or girlfriends?
Maybe the better question is no longer:
“How many hearts can I hold without technically sinning?”
Maybe it is:
“Jesus, how do I hold another person's heart without forgetting that it belongs first to You?”
Because someday, the person whose attention you are enjoying today may become somebody else's husband.
Somebody else's wife.
Somebody else's answered prayer.
Treat them accordingly.
Love does not need ambiguity to survive.
Truth does not need manipulation to keep someone interested.
And you do not need a collection of human hearts to prove that yours has value.
At the cross, Jesus already settled the question of how far divine love was willing to go to rescue sinners.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Tell the truth where truth has been avoided.
Release the people you have been keeping as options.
Forgive where you have been wounded.
Receive grace where shame has been screaming.
And let Christ teach you how to love without using, desire without possessing, discern without deceiving, and walk away without destroying.
Your romantic history does not have to become the final name of your story.
The chapter you are ashamed to reread may become the very page where Jesus begins writing redemption.
